title: Majestic
reviewNotes: Three comparisons are explicitly limited to the final seven-piece diagram after g2 at 147s. f6/g1=Q/f7 is actual mate; an independent knight underpromotion also fails to f7 mate. Independent Kd6 loses. Earlier larger rook skewer, h6 restraint and Ke7 sacrifice remain source context, not an exact proof of those decisions.
transcript: What's brilliant that he has king to E7, sacrificing the white rook completely. But of course if the rook is taken, now rook to F4 would be a checkmate. So black cannot do that. But black comes up with a counter brilliancy himself. Rook to E7 check, leaving the black knight to hang because once the knight falls, black is now going to be able to play rook to A7 and threaten a skewer of the king and rook. But not only that, if you check the black king, you're still going to lose the rook like this. There doesn't seem to be a way to [music] save this rook. If you come here and try to use the king after the skewer, you would still lose the rook. But white has another incredible idea. The very precise rook to H8. This still loses the rook after the skewer, but on white's terms. Because now white can play rook to F4 with a check and the only legal move is for the king to go to G8 and now be the one to block his own rook. But this not bother black. He's just going to be able to play H6, move the king [music] and then free up the rook. And at the very least this is going to be a draw, which is exactly why white plays pawn to H6, preventing that move from black. But the brilliant mind [music] of the player with the black pieces has not depleted all of his resources. And he finds pawn to G5 attacking the white rook and setting up an incredible trap. If you move the rook anywhere away from this file, the black king is going to be able to move and now free up the rook and you cannot check the king anymore. But if you try to save the rook by staying on this file, now this is actually a stalemate. Black [laughter] has no legal moves with any of his pieces, but he is not checkmated. So this would be a draw. So it seems like black has found the perfect way to save the game and he is is out of the woods, right? >> [music] >> Well, not exactly. Because in this position, white plays the incredible and majestic king to E7. And all of a sudden, black realizes that he is completely lost. You see, the [music] only legal move available to black is to take that rook. And this doesn't seem to make any sense. White is only left with two white pawns. And not only that, black is going to get a queen way faster than white. But you see, that doesn't matter. Because against a queen and a rook, it's the position to win the game. Because all that white needs is one pawn to deliver checkmate.
